groups.title: Three ground rules
groups.intro: These three rules decide many of the questions below at once. Sign them first, because every later answer is checked against them before the freeze.

items.title: Silent sources mean the rule does not apply
items.question: If the books for a style say nothing about a constraint, should the tool skip that rule for that style?
items.context: Some rules come from one style's books and are copied to the others by default. Example: 'the domain must not import a framework' is a Clean rule, and the Layered books never state it. P1 says such a rule is switched off in Layered, and no Layered-only substitute is made up.

options.label: Yes, confirm P1
options.effect: Decides Q1 and Q10. Rules a style's books never state are not applied to that style.

options.label: No, keep rules on by default
options.effect: Every rule applies to every style unless a source forbids it. Q1 and Q10 must be argued one by one.

items.why: It is your own principle in another form: a rule must come from the style's sources (ops/decisions.md, U6). A rule kept 'by default' has no source.
items.risk_note: Read strictly, P1 would also say no to Q16 (cycles in DDD); Q16 rests on ADP being general, not on P1.

items.title: One import edge, one rule
items.question: Should each bad import be reported under only the rule it actually breaks, not twice under two rules?
items.context: An import edge is one line like 'a file in persistence/ imports from business/'. Without P2 the same line can show up as a direction error and again as a cycle or a layer skip. P2 picks one owner per edge.

options.label: Yes, confirm P2
options.effect: Decides Q4, Q7, Q11, Q12 and Q20. Fewer duplicate findings. One declared exception remains: under Q6 B an application-to-adapter edge is reported by two rules.

options.label: No, allow double reports
options.effect: The same edge can count under several rules, so counts grow and Q4, Q7, Q12 and Q20 must be argued again.

items.why: The sources each state one constraint per clause (for example Fowler and POSA state 'no upward use' and 'no skipping' as two separate clauses), so one edge breaks one clause.
items.risk_note: Q6 B breaks P2 on purpose; the ADR must write that exception down.

items.title: The source beats the sealed wording
items.question: When a book says one thing and the sealed rule text says another, should the book win, through a declared ADR?
items.context: The sealed files were frozen before the source check of 2026-10-16. That check found three places where the sealed text and the books disagree: the DDD anti-corruption layer (Q18), the DDD 'every file in a context' rule (Q15) and domain-event placement (Q21). This item says which side wins.

options.label: Source wins, by a declared ADR
options.effect: Q15, Q18 and Q21 follow the books. Each change is one more declared post-seal deviation, listed with the others.

options.label: Sealed text wins
options.effect: Q15, Q18 and Q21 keep the sealed defaults. The thesis must say these three rules differ from Evans.

items.why: This is your stated principle (ops/decisions.md:23), and construct-decisions already says 'the source wins' over a rule's wording (Precedence, :26).
items.risk_note: Each source-following change adds a post-seal deviation, and an examiner counts deviations as a risk of their own.

groups.title: The 25 construct answers (V1)
groups.intro: Each question defines what one rule means, using the style's books. The freeze check (F3) refuses to run until all 25 [Answer]: lines in Docs/v1.3/construct-decisions.md are filled in.

items.title: Layered services may hold a data gateway
items.question: In a Layered project, may a business service keep a persistence object (a gateway) as a field without a finding?
items.context: FF-P06 (the domain-state-purity rule) flags domain code that holds an infrastructure object. In Layered, an OrderService holding an OrderGateway is the normal design. This fix is already in the tool; you are confirming it.

options.label: Yes, FF-P06 does not apply in Layered
options.effect: Keeps the current tool. 53 baseline findings stay gone; the Layered clean variant passes.

options.label: Keep it as a warning only
options.effect: No verdict changes, but Layered gets about 53 extra warnings.

options.label: Back to blocking, as in v1.2E
options.effect: The Layered clean example fails again; precision falls to 8/61.

items.why: Fowler (bliki, 2015) and Evans 2003 ch. 4 let the domain use the layer below, and the Layered sources state no isolated-domain rule, so P1 applies.
items.risk_note: Already built and checked; confirming changes nothing.

items.title: Type-only imports count as dependencies
items.question: Should an 'import type' line count as a dependency, the same as a normal import?
items.context: TypeScript can import a type that vanishes after compiling. Example: a domain entity with 'import type { Request } from express'. 12 findings rest only on such lines, most of them in DDD.

options.label: Yes, count them
options.effect: No change. The 12 findings stay.

options.label: No, ignore type-only imports
options.effect: 7 of DDD's 8 blocking findings disappear.

items.why: Martin's blog says an inner circle must not even mention an outer name ('functions, classes, variables'), and an import type mentions one.
items.risk_note: Strong verbatim source; no code change.

items.title: File cycles inside one layer
items.question: If two files in the same layer import each other, should that only be a warning, while cycles across layers still block?
items.context: FF-S02 (the no-cycles rule) comes from Martin's acyclic dependencies principle. Example: domain/Loan.ts imports domain/Member.ts and Member.ts imports Loan.ts. Martin states the principle for components (units you release), not for single files.

options.label: Every file cycle blocks
options.effect: No change; 4 in-layer cycles keep failing their projects.

options.label: Only cycles across layers or modules count
options.effect: The 4 in-layer cycles disappear completely.

options.label: In-layer cycles become warnings
options.effect: The 4 rows move to advisory; cross-layer cycles still block. Needs a tier ADR.

items.why: Martin (Clean Architecture ch. 12 and ch. 14, p. 112) defines ADP over components, so a file cycle inside one layer is only a stand-in for it, and a stand-in is advisory by the tier rules.
items.risk_note: It changes the rule's unit after the seal, so the thesis must state the unit; MEAN-01 R4 uses the same reading.

items.title: Layer cycles without a file cycle
items.question: If one upward import makes two layers depend on each other, but no files form a loop, should that also count as a cycle?
items.context: Example: domain/Loan.ts imports application/ports/Clock.ts. Since application already depends on domain, the layers now point both ways. FF-S01 (the direction rule) already reports that upward import.

options.label: No, the direction finding is enough
options.effect: No change. Adjudication rows #1 to #4 leave the reference.

options.label: Yes, also compute cycles between layers
options.effect: Recovers rows #1 to #4, but adds 11 more blocking rows the blind key does not list either.

items.why: Martin does not treat a layer as an ADP component, so the layer cycle adds no fact beyond the upward edge FF-S01 already reports (P2).
items.risk_note: Matches the source; the blind key disagrees on 4 rows, which the adjudication sheet handles.

items.title: Adapter importing another adapter
items.question: In Hexagonal and DDD, should a web controller that directly imports a database adapter fail the check, and under which rule?
items.context: Example: adapters/inbound/http/RoomController.ts imports adapters/outbound/persistence/InMemoryRoomRepository.ts, skipping the application. Today it is only FF-S03 (the layer-skip warning). Cockburn never writes 'adapters must not talk', and his own sample wires one adapter to another, so blocking is an inference from 'actors talk to the application through ports'.

options.label: Keep as a warning (sealed default)
options.effect: No change; the 2 planted adapter defects in hex and the ddd api-to-infrastructure row do not fail.

options.label: Make FF-S03 blocking in hex and ddd
options.effect: Same counts as C/D, but FF-S03 then means two different things.

options.label: Report it under FF-S01, blocking
options.effect: The edge breaks the spec's declared allowed dependencies, so the direction rule reports it. Scored natively by the existing scorers; hex +2, ddd +1 blocking.

options.label: New rule id FF-S05, blocking
options.effect: Cleanest naming, but the registered scorers do not know FF-S05, so it shows no gain unless the scorers are changed too (G0.8 a), which is one more deviation.

items.why: The sealed Hexagonal source row says each actor talks to the application through a port, and the spec does not allow inbound-to-outbound edges, so FF-S01 is the spec-derived owner. The source check (rule-source-verification, Q5) says to label it 'stricter than Cockburn' and exempt wiring code, which the composition-layer exclusion already does. The sheet's default is D; C gives the same construct without a scorer change.
items.risk_note: An inference, not a quotation, and every real hex/ddd repo with adapter-to-adapter imports gains blocking findings; the MO-H03 fresh check (G0.9) can withdraw it.

items.title: Is the application layer inside the hexagon
items.question: In Hexagonal, should an application service that imports an adapter break core isolation, just like a domain file would?
items.context: FF-S04 (the core-isolation rule) today guards only domain/. Example: application/services/CancelBookingService.ts imports adapters/inbound/http/HttpTypes. The phrase 'application core' that the old text quoted is not in Cockburn; his hexagon is the whole application with no inner split.

options.label: No, the core is domain only
options.effect: No change.

options.label: Yes, core = domain + application
options.effect: Adds FF-S04 on 2 hex rows (FF-S01 already blocks them, so no new edge is found), and drops the agreed hex v02 FF-S04 row (see N1). Two rules then own app-to-adapter edges.

items.why: Cockburn's 'Intent' and 'Nature of the Solution' describe the hexagon as the application itself, not split into domain and application; the substance favours B even without the wrong quotation.
items.risk_note: It only relabels edges FF-S01 already blocks, and it breaks P2 on purpose; the ADR must name both FF-S01 and FF-S04 as owners.

items.title: Using a concrete adapter breaks the port rule
items.question: Should code that uses a concrete repository class (instead of its interface) also count as breaking the port-adapter placement rule?
items.context: FF-P03 (the port-placement rule) checks where an interface and its implementation live. Example: FindAvailableRoomsService takes an InMemoryRoomRepository instead of a RoomRepository port. The direction rule and FF-P02 (the dependency-inversion rule) already report this.

options.label: No, other rules already own it
options.effect: No change. Adjudication rows #7, #10, #13 leave the reference.

options.label: Yes, also report FF-P03
options.effect: +3 rows found, but +4 blocking false alarms.

items.why: Martin ch. 22-23 and Cockburn describe where the implementer lives; Martin ch. 11 (DIP) covers the user of a concrete class, and that is FF-P02's job (P2).
items.risk_note: Well supported; the wording 'sources silent on consumers' should be corrected in the ADR.

items.title: Objects created in a field initializer
items.question: When a domain class creates an infrastructure object in a field ('private clock = new SystemClock()'), should that half of the rule be reported as not measured, as the sealed text says?
items.context: FF-P06 (the domain-state rule) has two halves: objects passed in the constructor, and objects created in fields. The tool barely records the second kind of fact. All 3 detections come from that thin half.

options.label: Score them as blocking
options.effect: Contradicts the sealed note; needs an ADR. Keeps 3 blocking rows.

options.label: Report that half as N/A
options.effect: The 3 rows are listed as 'recall unestimated', not scored. The constructor half still blocks.

items.why: The sealed tier text says only the constructor half is valid and the other half is reported N/A; the source supplement records FF-P06 as 'blocking, constructor half only'. Source and sealed text agree here.
items.risk_note: Every U6 figure already assumes B; the owning unit must confirm it.

items.title: Repository missing its 'implements' clause
items.question: If a repository class drops 'implements LoanRepository' but still fits the interface, should the port-placement rule flag it?
items.context: TypeScript accepts any class with the right shape. Example: 'export class InMemoryLoanRepository {' with no implements. FF-P03 flags it today; FF-P02 does not.

options.label: FF-P03 yes, FF-P02 no
options.effect: No change.

options.label: Both rules flag it
options.effect: Blocking counts unchanged; 4 more warnings.

options.label: Neither, shape match is enough
options.effect: 3 blocking rows disappear in clean, nestjs and hex.

items.why: Martin's inversion (ch. 11 and 22) is a source-code dependency from the implementation to the interface, and without 'implements' that dependency is absent.
items.risk_note: No code change.

items.title: Framework imports in Layered business code
items.question: In a Layered project, should the domain-purity rule be switched off, with only web-framework imports caught as an upward dependency?
items.context: FF-P01 (the domain-purity rule) forbids framework imports in the domain. Example: business/model/Order.ts uses the typeorm @Entity decorator, and business/services/OrderService.ts imports express. Fowler's Layered style lets business code use persistence (Active Record), but business code must not depend on the presentation layer above it.

options.label: Purity applies to every framework
options.effect: No change; typeorm and express both fail.

options.label: Purity for web frameworks only
options.effect: Invents a Layered-only package list no source states.

options.label: Purity off; express etc. mapped to presentation
options.effect: typeorm is allowed; express becomes an FF-S01 upward-direction finding through a fixed package-to-layer list (express, koa, fastify). A new mechanism.

options.label: Purity off, no replacement
options.effect: Both typeorm and express are allowed in Layered business code; loses one blind row (#5).

items.why: P1 (no purity row for Layered; Fowler's Active Record) switches FF-P01 off, and Fowler PoEAA ch. 1 says the domain 'should never be dependent on the presentation' (recalled, check the page), which makes the express case a direction fact.
items.risk_note: The package-to-layer list is the most fit-prone item in U6 and is close to a hand-written rule; G0.9 sends it to D if the external-repo check finds a wrong row.

items.title: Domain must not import application code
items.question: In Hexagonal and DDD, should a domain file that imports from the application layer still be a violation?
items.context: Example: ordering/domain/customer/Customer.ts imports PlaceOrderCommand from ../../application. Both specs split domain from application.

options.label: Yes, forbidden by FF-S01
options.effect: No change; FF-S04 stays out of DDD.

options.label: No, the core is one unit
options.effect: 1 hex and 1 ddd blocking row disappear.

items.why: Evans (DDD Reference 2015 and the 2003 book) and Martin both put the domain below the application layer.
items.risk_note: Verbatim support; no code change.

items.title: Upward import is not a layer skip
items.question: In Layered, should an upward import between neighbouring layers be reported only as a direction error, not also as a 'skipped layer'?
items.context: Example: persistence/ProductGateway.ts imports business/model/Money. It goes up, but skips nothing. Today it is reported twice, as FF-S01 and FF-S03 (the layer-skip rule).

options.label: Report both rules
options.effect: No change; 2 duplicate rows stay.

options.label: FF-S03 only for downward skips
options.effect: 2 Layered false alarms go away; the direction finding stays.

items.why: Fowler and POSA state two clauses ('lower layers do not use upper ones'; strict layering 'also forbids skipping'), and an upward edge breaks only the first (P2).
items.risk_note: It can only remove rows; G0.9 checks that no real violation is lost.

items.title: NestJS services may import repositories
items.question: In NestJS, should a service that imports a repository class be allowed, as the NestJS preset's layer order says?
items.context: The NestJS preset declares Controller -> Service -> Repository. ADR-V13-02 wrongly calls it 'Clean layering'. Example: registrations.service.ts imports InMemoryRegistrationRepository.

options.label: Preset order; leave FF-P04 as is
options.effect: No blocking change; an advisory rule keeps contradicting the order.

options.label: Preset order; FF-P04 follows it
options.effect: Same blocking counts; one advisory false alarm goes; fix the ADR-V13-02 wording.

options.label: Clean order, infrastructure outermost
options.effect: Recovers row #6 but loses an agreed nestjs v02 row; needs Q25 B or precision collapses.

items.why: The preset states the order, and the NestJS docs' own TypeORM example injects a repository into a service. Before sealing, fix ADR-V13-02's 'Clean layering' claim and re-check that FF-P06 and FF-P07 in nestjs still hold on the preset's own order.
items.risk_note: Fixing ADR-V13-02 removes the 'Clean reading' that FF-P06, FF-S04 and FF-P07 use to block in nestjs; those must be re-argued from the preset order.

items.title: Value objects must be immutable
items.question: Should the value-object immutability rule keep blocking, now that the tool also reads readonly fields and setters?
items.context: FF-DT03 (the immutable-value-object rule). Example: Quantity.ts has 'set value(v) { this.current = v; }'. The extractor used to miss accessors; member facts have since been added (the after-member-facts run).

options.label: Blocking; unseen half reported N/A
options.effect: g01 is listed as 'not measured' rather than a miss.

options.label: Warning until the facts exist
options.effect: Rule stops failing verdicts.

options.label: Blocking, with member facts in the extractor
options.effect: g01 becomes a hit; ddd 10/10. No tier ADR needed, only a note.

items.why: Evans (DDD Reference p. 12) says 'Treat the value object as immutable' without exception; use A for any part the extractor still cannot see. Note Evans 2003's performance exception in the thesis.
items.risk_note: Sheet default is 'A, becoming C'; choose C only if the member facts are merged on main.

items.title: Every DDD file inside a context
items.question: Should a DDD file that sits outside every bounded context (like src/utils/formatCurrency.ts) be only a warning, not a failure?
items.context: FF-DS01 (the every-file-in-a-context rule) has no row in the sealed tier table; its blocking tier came from early DDD notes. Evans says contexts need explicit boundaries and shared model code must be designated, but never that every file must belong to a context.

options.label: Keep blocking, decide later (sheet default)
options.effect: A rule with no sealed tier row can fail a verdict; must be reported apart in the hold-out (prespec line 59).

options.label: Warning, with its own tier row by ADR
options.effect: ddd v07 stops failing; FF-DS02 still blocks any cross-context import.

items.why: Source and default disagree: the source check calls FF-DS01 'the weakest blocking rule' because Evans (DDD Reference pp. 2, 31) never says every file belongs to a context, so the rule is a project convention, which the tier rules make advisory. By PREC, the source wins.
items.risk_note: It is one more ADR, and 'defer' would leave an unsourced blocking rule in force at the freeze.

items.title: DDD projects get the no-cycles rule
items.question: Should DDD projects also be checked for import cycles, like Clean and Layered ones?
items.context: Example: PlaceOrder -> CustomerRepository -> Customer -> PlaceOrder is a real three-file loop in ddd v09 that nothing reported. ADR-V14-01 already added FF-S02 to DDD; this records the answer.

options.label: No cycle rule for DDD
options.effect: Contradicts ADR-V14-01, which is already built.

options.label: Yes, add FF-S02, blocking
options.effect: Records what ADR-V14-01 did; one development run, no second tuning loop.

items.why: Martin states ADP for components in general (Clean Architecture Part IV, ch. 14), not for one style.
items.risk_note: Settled in substance by ADR-V14-01; only the answer line is missing.

items.title: Importing through a context's index file
items.question: If one context imports another context's code through that context's index.ts, should that count as using its public API?
items.context: Example: billing imports GetOrderSummary from ordering/index.ts (allowed) versus straight from ordering/application/GetOrderSummary.ts (flagged). The index file is the context's declared public face.

options.label: Yes, the index is the public API
options.effect: No change.

options.label: No, judge the real target file
options.effect: g02 becomes a violation too.

options.label: Yes, plus a warning for exposed services
options.effect: Same blocking counts; one new advisory rule.

items.why: Sources silent on re-exports (Evans's Open Host Service is just 'a protocol... as a set of services'), so the context's own declaration decides.
items.risk_note: Already the tool's behaviour.

items.title: Anti-corruption layer reaching upstream internals
items.question: Should a DDD translation layer (ACL) be forced to use the other context's public API, instead of importing its internal files?
items.context: An anti-corruption layer translates another context's model. Example: billing/acl/OrderingAcl.ts imports ordering/domain/order/value-objects/OrderId.js, an internal file. The sealed rule text exempts ACL folders; Evans says the ACL talks to the other system 'through its existing interface'.

options.label: Exempt the ACL (sealed default)
options.effect: No change; n01 stays clean. The thesis must say the rule is broader than Evans.

options.label: ACL must use the public API
options.effect: n01 becomes a blocking FF-DS02 finding; ddd 9/9.

items.why: Sealed default and source disagree: Evans (DDD Reference 2015, p. 34) says the ACL 'talks to the other system through its existing interface'. By your principle the source wins, so B.
items.risk_note: Changes a sealed rule's wording after seeing the data, so it needs an ADR that cites p. 34 as the reason.

items.title: Any import of an aggregate's inner entity
items.question: Should any outside import of an aggregate's inner entity count, even though Evans allows short-lived use?
items.context: FF-DT01 (the aggregate-boundary rule). Example: an application file imports OrderLine instead of going through the Order root. An import cannot show whether the reference is kept or only used briefly.

options.label: Yes, labelled 'stricter than Evans'
options.effect: No change; the thesis states the stricter reading.

options.label: Only references that are kept
options.effect: The tool cannot check this, so the ddd v01 row disappears.

items.why: Evans (DDD Reference p. 16) allows transient references, so A is a declared stricter reading; B is the source as written but cannot be checked from imports.
items.risk_note: Strictly the source favours B; A survives only because it is labelled and unimplementable otherwise.

items.title: Framework reached through one extra hop
items.question: Should the domain-purity rule look only at direct framework imports, not frameworks reached through another file?
items.context: Example: domain/registration-policy.ts imports a repository file, and that file imports @nestjs/common. The direction rules already report the domain-to-repository import.

options.label: Direct imports only
options.effect: No change; adjudication row #8 leaves the reference.

options.label: Count indirect imports too
options.effect: Recovers nothing here and adds 14 blocking false alarms.

items.why: Martin and Evans are silent on indirect dependencies, and the indirect part is already a direction fault owned by FF-S01 and FF-S04 (P2).
items.risk_note: No code change.

items.title: Domain events must live in the domain
items.question: Should a domain-event class placed outside the domain layer fail the check, not just warn?
items.context: FF-DT05 (the event-placement rule). Example: billing/application/InvoiceIssued.ts implements DomainEvent but sits in application/. The sealed table calls this a guideline, but Evans's 2015 Reference says an event is part of the domain model and domain code lives in one layer.

options.label: Warning, as sealed
options.effect: No change. The reason 'no source states it' must be corrected.

options.label: Blocking, by ADR
options.effect: ddd v05 fails on this rule too (both keys already list the row).

items.why: Sealed default and source disagree: Evans (DDD Reference p. 13) 'Represent each event as a domain object' and p. 10 'Concentrate all the code related to the domain model in one layer'. By PREC the source wins.
items.risk_note: It is a two-step inference, and the rule cannot tell a domain event from a system event that wrongly implements the declared type; A stays defensible if you reject PREC.

items.title: Injecting a sibling service in NestJS
items.question: Should the dependency-inversion warning ignore a NestJS service that injects another service of the same layer?
items.context: FF-P02 (the dependency-inversion warning) counts injected concrete classes. Example: RegistrationsService injects WorkshopsService. NestJS docs show this as standard practice. The rule is advisory only.

options.label: Count every injected class
options.effect: No change; one advisory false alarm stays.

options.label: Count only other layers
options.effect: The near-miss false alarm goes; thesis says FF-P02 is DIP across layers only.

items.why: The NestJS docs ('Providers') show same-layer injection as the style's norm; this is stated as a narrowing of Martin's general DIP (ch. 11), which is not boundary-scoped.
items.risk_note: Advisory only, but it narrows Martin after a false alarm, so the thesis must call it a narrowing.

items.title: What counts as an entity
items.question: Should the tool treat a class as an entity because it lives in the declared entity folder, rather than because its name ends in 'Entity'?
items.context: FF-P05 (an advisory entity rule). Example: domain/entities/Loan.ts is an entity but has no 'Entity' suffix, so the tool misses it today.

options.label: By name suffix
options.effect: No change; two advisory rows stay missed.

options.label: By the declared layer or folder
options.effect: Two advisory rows are found; template change.

items.why: Sources silent → the spec decides, and the spec declares entities by folder (domain/entities/**).
items.risk_note: Advisory only.

items.title: Controllers using domain types directly
items.question: Should it be allowed for an outer adapter to use an inner domain type directly, skipping the use-case layer?
items.context: Example: RoomController calls DateRange.parse from domain/model. The dependency points inward, which the styles allow.

options.label: Not a finding
options.effect: No change; 5 advisory or unscored rows stay out.

options.label: Advisory FF-S03 finding
options.effect: Adds a few advisory rows in hex and clean.

items.why: Martin's circles constrain direction only, and the sealed FF-S03 reason says inward skipping is allowed outside Layered.
items.risk_note: No blocking effect.

items.title: Declare roles for wiring and stray files
items.question: Should the presets say outright how the tool treats files like main.ts, NestJS module files and test containers?
items.context: Wiring files (composition roots) import everything by design. Today they stay silent only because no folder pattern happens to match them. A future project could trigger them by accident.

options.label: Leave as is
options.effect: No change now; behaviour stays an accident of the folder patterns.

options.label: Declare them in the presets
options.effect: A 'composition-root' role exempt from layer rules; folder beats file name. One development run, no second tuning.

items.why: Sources mostly silent (Martin ch. 26 'Main' treats the wiring component as outside the layers), so the spec should state the behaviour rather than leave it to chance.
items.risk_note: A preset change after scoring; anything surprising in its one run goes into an ADR, not code.

groups.title: Two new rules added after the seal (ADR-V14-01 and -02)
groups.intro: Two rules were added after the inputs were frozen: cycle checking for DDD, and FF-P07 (no web framework in application code). Their open parts are marked Proposed and only count in the hold-out if signed before the freeze.

items.title: How the DDD cycle rule is added
items.question: Should the DDD cycle rule be added by a switch that runs only in the new v1.3 scoring mode, leaving the frozen DDD preset file untouched?
items.context: The DDD preset file is hashed in the sealed inputs, so editing it would break the seal. The overlay adds FF-S02 at compile time instead, and old saved results keep their old scores.

options.label: Overlay, v1.3 mode only
options.effect: Every new DDD run is scored with cycles; frozen files and old figures stay the same.

options.label: Edit presets/ddd.yaml
options.effect: Simpler to read, but changes a sealed file's hash.

items.why: The sealed FF-S02 tier row ('acyclic dependencies principle; a structural fact') has no style exception, and Martin's ADP is general; the overlay changes membership only.
items.risk_note: Already built and tested; Q3's answer will also split DDD cycles.

items.title: Which packages application code must avoid
items.question: Should FF-P07 forbid only HTTP server packages (express, fastify, koa, hapi, restify, Nest platform packages) in application code?
items.context: FF-P07 (the application-purity rule) flags a use case that imports the web framework, e.g. 'import { Request } from express' in application/. @nestjs/common, ORMs, DI and validation libraries stay allowed, because every NestJS service needs @Injectable.

options.label: HTTP delivery packages only
options.effect: The planted framework-leak seeds are caught; NestJS services stay clean.

options.label: Every declared framework
options.effect: Fires on every NestJS application service (13 fixture files).

items.why: Martin (Clean Architecture ch. 21) says 'the Web is a delivery mechanism' and Cockburn says the use case does not know the delivery mechanism; Martin's broader 'frameworks are details' (ch. 32) is qualified by Martin himself.
items.risk_note: The list was narrowed after counting fixture matches, and the seeds plant express, so catching them proves nothing on its own.

items.title: FF-P07 blocks in four styles
items.question: Should a web-framework import in application code fail the check in Clean, Hexagonal, NestJS and DDD?
